newsitem.title: USA: FAA tests U.S. airports' altitude warning systems.
newsitem.headline: FAA tests U.S. airports' altitude warning systems.

text.p: Tests of altitude warning systems at 193 U.S. airports turned up errors in computer software functions at two of them, the Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday.

The FAA tested the minimum safe altitude warning systems at U.S. airports after the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation of the Korean Air Lines (KAL) accident in Guam last week raised questions about the performance of the system at the Pacific island's airport.
The KAL Boeing 747 was carrying 254 people when it crashed into a hill minutes before landing. Twenty-eight people survived.
The FAA said that as a routine precaution, it had ordered the testing and recertificiation of the altitude warning systems at U.S. airports.
The agency found software errors at Fayetteville, North Carolina, and Florence, South Carolina.
"These have been corrected and recertified," the FAA said.
The FAA said the system at the Aspen, Colorado, airport had been certified but was not in service because of the many low-altitude false alerts in the mountainous terrain.
"Aviators have been notified of this condition," the FAA said.
The altitude software warns controllers when planes are flying or are about to fly below minimum safe altitudes.
